issues.legal_issue: A supervisory petition challenging a subordinate court’s decree is ordinarily not entertained when an adequate and more comprehensive appeal is available and no extraordinary circumstances justify intervention.
material_facts: The respondent challenged a decree of the City Civil Court through a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution instead of pursuing an available appeal to the High Court.
The available appeal was adequate and more comprehensive than the supervisory remedy.
The case presented no extraordinary circumstances warranting supervisory intervention.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the supervisory petition; its order was set aside and the petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 227 of the Constitution, supervisory jurisdiction is extraordinary, must be exercised sparingly, and is not appellate jurisdiction. The High Court ordinarily declines to exercise it when an adequate alternative legal remedy is available, although extraordinary circumstances may justify intervention. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: supervisory_petition_challenges_decree and adequate_appeal_available and not extraordinary_circumstances

predicates.supervisory_petition_challenges_decree: A party challenges a subordinate court’s decree by seeking supervisory intervention.
predicates.adequate_appeal_available: The party has an available appeal that provides an adequate remedy at least as comprehensive as the supervisory remedy.
predicates.extraordinary_circumstances: Circumstances exist that exceptionally justify supervisory intervention despite the available appeal.
predicates.supervisory_petition_dismissed: The supervisory petition is not entertained and is dismissed.

issues.definition: When a party uses supervisory proceedings to challenge a decree despite an adequate appeal, and no exceptional circumstances justify intervention, the supervisory petition is dismissed.

issues.legal_issue: A supervisory court cannot decide in advance whether a judgment will bind parties in a separate pending proceeding when that question has not yet been determined in that proceeding.
material_facts: A separate suit concerning the same dispute was pending in the Small Causes Court.
The High Court directed that the City Civil Court’s decision should not bind the parties in the pending suit.

The Small Causes Court had not yet decided whether the City Civil Court’s decision would bind the parties, and no decision on that question had been brought before the High Court in an appeal or revision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not pre-empt the Small Causes Court’s determination; that court had to decide the question in the pending suit, subject to appeal if its decision was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: A court should determine a question arising in a proceeding before it, and a higher court should not pronounce on that question before the lower court has decided it and the decision has been brought before the higher court by appeal or revision. The judgment discusses Article 227 of the Constitution but relies on no earlier cases or specific provision for this conclusion.

predicates.supervisory_proceeding_concerns_judgment: A party asks a supervisory court to determine the effect of a judgment in a separate suit that is still pending.
predicates.pending_suit_court_has_not_decided_judgm: The court hearing the pending suit has not yet decided whether the judgment affects the parties in that suit.
predicates.no_appeal_or_revision_from_that_decision: No decision on the judgment’s effect has been brought before the supervisory court by appeal or revision.
predicates.supervisory_court_must_not_pronounce_jud: The supervisory court must leave the judgment’s effect for determination in the pending suit.

issues.definition: When a separate suit is pending and its court has not decided the effect of a prior judgment, the supervisory court must leave that question for the pending suit rather than decide it in advance.
